answer.summary: Ellis said Dropbox already had an amazing referral rate before its incentive program: the program accelerated existing word of mouth, but couldn’t make people talk about a product they didn’t want to share.

sections.heading: Dropbox’s example
sections.content: Ellis’s point was that Dropbox’s referral program did not create people’s willingness to recommend the product from scratch. Dropbox already had an “amazing referral rate” before the program; incentives could accelerate that behavior, but would not fix a product people did not want to talk about. He warned that companies copying Dropbox by simply adding referral incentives may miss that prerequisite.
